rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A prism deviates a ray toward its base. The deviation is least when the passage is symmetric, and the index is then sin((A+δ_m)/2) divided by sin(A/2). A 60° prism of index √2 has a minimum deviation of 30°. Violet, with the higher index, is deviated more than red.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ state the rule without its limit → ✅ note when it applies / stops applying.  ·  ❌ no diagram → ✅ add one labelled figure / structured list.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: For A = 60° and μ = √2, δ_m = 30°.  ·  Angles in the sine formula are in degrees only after you take the sine of those degrees.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: A triangular prism has apex angle A. A ray that enters one face and leaves the other is bent toward the base if the prism's index is higher than the surrounding air.  ·  Inside the prism the two refraction angles at the faces add to the apex angle: A = r1 + r2. The total deviation δ is i + e − A, where i is the angle of incidence and e is the angle of emergence.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: refraction through prisms — angle of deviation, minimum deviation (within Ray Optics).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: At minimum deviation, i = e.  ·  μ from the sine formula, not from A alone.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Write μ in terms of A and δ_m.  ·  What is special about the ray at minimum deviation?

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Prism deviation  ·  Minimum deviation  ·  Index formula  ·  Dispersion

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Refraction through prisms — angle of deviation  ·  A prism deviates light toward the base.  ·  Deviation depends on the angle and the index.  ·  Minimum deviation is the symmetric case.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Lens maker: 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). Power P = 1/f (dioptre, f in metres); lenses add powers in contact.  ·  Refraction at a plane surface (Snell): n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂. Total internal reflection when θ > θ_c, sinθ_c = n₂/n₁ (n₂<n₁).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Which colour is deviated more?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A prism has A = 60° and μ = √2. Show that the angle of minimum deviation is 30°.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Inside the prism → A  ·  At minimum deviation → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: As the prism is rotated, the deviation falls to a minimum and then rises. At minimum deviation the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base for an isosceles prism, and i = e.  ·  Then r1 = r2 = A/2, and the index is μ = sin((A + δ_m)/2) / sin(A/2). Measuring A and the angle of minimum deviation is a standard way to find μ.  ·  A larger index means a larger minimum deviation for the same prism. Violet is deviated more than red because its index is higher. That spread is dispersion.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The index is found from A and δ_m.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ lens maker: 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂). power p = 1/f (dioptre, f in metres); lenses add powers in contact..  ·  Deviation is not the apex angle.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Minimum deviation is the symmetric passage.  ·  The thin-prism formula is not the general one.  ·  Violet deviates more than red.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Use the minimum-deviation position for the index experiment.  ·  Do not add δ to A and call it the index.  ·  Write A = r1 + r2 and say what each symbol means.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mark the known values, then substitute one step at a time.  ·  Finish with the number, the unit, and the direction when the quantity has one.  ·  Prism minimum deviation: n = sin((A + D_min)/2)/sin(A/2). Achromatic doublet pairs crown (low Abbe) + flint (high Abbe).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: lens maker: 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂). power p = 1/f (dioptre, f in metres); lenses add powers in contact.  ·  A thin prism has a small A, and the deviation is approximately (μ − 1) A when the angles are in the same unit. That approximation is not the minimum-deviation formula.
